Equivocity
ē-kwĭ-vŏs´ĭ-tē
n. (the claim that a word is said of God and the creature in wholly different senses, so that the shared sound is a pun)
Latin aequivocus, of equal voice and unequal meaning, from aequus + vox. If univocity makes God a being among beings, equivocity makes every predicate a homonym. The analogical middle is the dictionary's path because Scripture talks and forbids likeness in the same breath.

Biblical Definition

Equivocity is the claim that our words about God share only a sound with our words about the world. Scripture refuses both the flattening and the gag. Moses is told the secret things belong to the Lord, and the revealed things belong to us: “The secret things belong unto the Lord our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever” (Deu 29:29). God speaks so as to be understood: “I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth” (Isa 45:19). And yet no man has seen Him: “No man hath seen God at any time” (John 1:18). Paul does not conclude silence. He concludes gift: “the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God. Now we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God” (1Co 2:11–12). Equivocity would make that reception a noise. The Spirit makes it knowledge.

Origin & Era

Webster (1828) defines equivocal as being of doubtful signification, and equivocation as the use of words of doubtful meaning. In the schools, equivocity is the claim that God-talk and creature-talk share a sound only.

expand to see more

EQUIVOCAL, a. [L. aequivocus; aequus, equal, and vox, word.]

Being of doubtful signification; that may be understood in different senses.

EQUIVOCATION, n. Ambiguity of speech; the use of words or expressions that are susceptible of a double signification.

Theological equivocity is stronger: the claim that the shared word is a mere homonym when said of God.

Key Scripture

Deu 29:29 — "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law."

Isa 45:19 — "I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth: I said not unto the seed of Jacob, Seek ye me in vain: I the LORD speak righteousness, I declare things that are right."

John 1:18 — "No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him."

1Co 2:11 — "For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him? even so the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God."

1Co 2:12 — "Now we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God."

Modern Corruption

Equivocity is used to keep God ineffable by making revelation a shrug, and Deuteronomy 29:29 already divided the secret from the revealed.

expand to see more

A certain apophatic fashion treats every predicate as an honour paid to silence. Isaiah 45:19 will not have it. I have not spoken in secret. The God of Israel is not the unknown god. He has talked in the open, and the talking is for keeping, not for guessing.

Deuteronomy 29:29 is the map the schools keep redrawing. Secret things belong unto the Lord. Revealed things belong unto us and to our children. Equivocity collapses the second column into the first. Then the confession becomes a mood, and the children inherit a hush.

First Corinthians 2 is why the dictionary will not take the gag. No man knows the things of God, but the Spirit of God, and we have received the Spirit that we might know what is freely given. Knowledge is gift, not univocal climb and not equivocal shrug. Analogia fidei is the name of that gift when it is reading Scripture by Scripture.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin aequivocus; Hebrew sathar (H5641), to hide, secret things; Greek apokalupto (G601), to reveal.

expand to see more

Latin aequivocus — equal voice, unequal sense; the homonym claim.

Hebrew nistaroth (H5641) — secret things; Deuteronomy 29:29, they belong unto the Lord.

Greek ginosko (G1097) — to know; 1 Corinthians 2:12, that we might know the things freely given.

Usage

"“Those things which are revealed belong unto us” — not a shrug."

"“I have not spoken in secret” — the opposite of equivocal theology."

"“That we might know” — gift, not a pun."
